title: Duncan Lennox - Off the Shelf AI Hit a Wall. Here's What HubSpot Did to Solve It.

segments.text: DUNCAN LENNOX: Good morning.
It's great to be here with you all.
I'd like to take you on a little bit of a journey
that we've been on at HubSpot over the last three years or so,
leveraging AI not only in what we build for our customers,
but also how we built it.
We've hit a few walls along the way, learned some lessons,
and I'd like to share those with you.
Firstly, to give you a little bit of context,
if you don't know a lot about HubSpot,
we just celebrated our 20th anniversary last month,
and we build a go-to-market platform for largely small
and medium-sized businesses and enterprises.
And that means we're building software that helps marketing,
sales, and service teams across that full go-to-market journey
as they bring their products and services to their customers.
And we have over 300,000 businesses today that depend
on HubSpot for their go-to-market journey in about
140 countries across dozens of industries.
And that means we get a view into what's
going on across a wide variety of companies of different scales
and in different regions.
So with that, what do we hear back mostly from customers
today?
It's the word "actually" inserted into this question
that's been around for the last couple of years.
How do I actually transform with AI,
not just run pilots, not just play around with it,
but actually deliver real value at scale for the company?
And what we've found over the last three plus
years on the journey we've been on
is that the tools themselves and toolchains are just
a starting point.
They're not enough.
And how you approach it makes a big difference.
And one of the big, somewhat unexpected learnings for us
over the whole process is we were
focusing on initially how do we build differently with AI?
And it turns out a lot of those learnings
apply to what we need to build for our customers
and how we need to meet them on their journey.
So what happened is we started back in 2023 or so
with the early stage copilot.
We'd moved beyond Code Assist into the early stage copilots.
But what we found was those systems off the shelf
couldn't work at our scale.
So we were doing about, at the time,
about a million builds a day across over 10,000
microservices.
It's more now.
And we were just running into walls.
And a lot of it was around the models being
very good at understanding coding problems generally
but not understanding enough about our business
and how we work.
And we had to address that.
We could wait for companies to catch up,
the tooling companies to catch up,
or we could dive in and try and solve the problem ourselves.
And that's what we chose to do.
And there's really three learnings
that came out of that that I want to share with you today.
And they're around flexible infrastructure, and complete
and trustworthy context, and then the notion of meeting
customers where they are.
So let's dive into the first one, flexible infrastructure.
So we started out with these copilots, as I mentioned.
And what we found pretty quickly is
they didn't understand nearly enough about our tools
and toolchain.
We had over a decade of building our own custom tools
and toolchains.
And of course, models are trained
on data that's out there in the world
and didn't have any access to how our particular tools worked.
So unsurprisingly, they struggled a little bit
with that.
So what we did there was we built a bunch
of MCP integrations in the very early days
of MCP that allowed us to bring more knowledge about how
our environment worked directly into the copilots themselves.
We also, pretty early on, built what
we would now call an agent execution platform or an agent
harness.
We actually built a containerized approach
that made it very easy for us to spin up sandboxes, where
test loops could run in an entirely automated way,
without any human intervention.
And that made it very lightweight for our engineers
and very safe and secure from a reliability and security
point of view as well.
And overall through this whole process, one of the things
we didn't do was mandate engineers that they
had to use AI and how they built.
We really wanted to take engineers on the journey,
show them how different and powerful an experience that is,
and have them adopt them themselves.
And it turned out, one of the big blockers to that
was engineers were very concerned about reliability.
We put a lot of time and energy into building an incredibly
reliable platform because it's mission
critical for the go-to-market teams in our customers.
And engineers were concerned it was going to introduce
reliability issues.
So we brought data.
We looked at what was happening with some of the early areas
where copilots and beyond were being used,
and we were able to show our own engineers that there was not
an impact on reliability, that reliability remained neutral
despite the addition of code generation coming
from these other platforms.
And in fact, skipping ahead for a moment,
today, where we are today, is reliability
is actually increasing with the result of agentic coding
and how we do it today.
And those early wins got us to about 80%
adoption, which is pretty good-- this is three years ago--
across our thousands of engineers
and about a 51% improvement overall
in productivity and velocity.
That's a composite metric measured
from a variety of different things
because we don't like to overrotate
on a single metric, like PRs or lines of code.
But we knew we could do more.
And of course, the technology was advancing as well.
So when we started building this infrastructure, as I mentioned,
one of the interesting things is we
started to learn that it actually
had a big impact or potential impact
on how we build for our customers as well.
So one of the lessons that we're able to bring to customers
is you really can't depend on a single vendor or model
family for everything.
Not only are the models obviously changing and improving
all the time, it's a little bit of a horse race,
but they're jagged in different areas.
And when you apply them into very specific areas
as we do with go-to-market, we find
that different models, model sizes, vendors
are better, right tool for the right job.
So we were pretty early to this notion
of we need a way to run evals, to do A/B tests against model
sizes.
And it's not as simple as quality or evals overall.
We think in terms of a mix of three things, quality, latency,
and cost, in that order of priority,
and solving for that because every individual task
within the hundreds go-to-market tasks
that we build agents for today actually has a different value
proposition around those three.
Some are low-stakes, where the quality bar does not
have to be quite as high, even though it's still high,
but it's a bulk process and cost optimization
is super important, even early on.
And then there's other tasks that are very high stakes,
particularly when the HubSpot platform is going
to do something that interacts with one of our customer's
customers, for example.
So that was one.
And so we built this abstraction layer, again,
today, what we would call an agent harness.
And it's a lot more sophisticated in 2026
than it was in 2023.
But that allows us to very easily, under the hood,
swap out models, do those evals, do those regression tests,
and comparisons against them.
And that's proved to be incredibly powerful.
And we built that abstraction layer
in a way that frees feature teams up
from having to be involved in any of the plumbing that goes
on underneath to support that.
They can create their evals.
They can run them against a variety of models, swap models
in and out with no regressions, without having
to be involved in any of that.
And that's turned out to be a huge advantage for us
in building for our customers and then delivering
what they need.
So at the end of the day, that's really
all about the shared foundation.
Do that first, not last.
I say that because often when you're trying to get going
and you think about lean or you think about getting to MVP,
there's a temptation to use a single stack for everything.
What we found is that it is a little bit
counterintuitive to that.
That energy put in up front around things
like harnesses, that gives you much more control
over your own destiny.
Your ability to do these evals and swap models in and out,
to be able to make changes to how an agentic loop runs,
is incredibly powerful.
And it's worth doing that early on.
And of course, today it's a lot easier to do that.
There's a lot of phenomenal solutions out there.
Companies like Fireworks are doing amazing work
in this space.
That's number one.
Number two, let's talk about context.
And we very deliberately talk about the comprehensive nature
of it and the trustworthy nature of it.
So when we were building initially
and we moved on to autonomous coding agents,
the agents needed to understand, of course, our code base,
our conventions, and the environment.
And we had all of this tooling that we'd been building
over the last decade as well.
And we had to get beyond even MCP here, allowing the coding
agents to be able to understand everything about how
our build chain worked.
And a lot of the time and energy that we had to put in there
to get much more effectiveness out of even frontier models
was backfilling all of that context and bringing it to bear.
And getting context right is hard.
It's not a matter of just hitting a context window limit
or dealing with context drift.
It's also the fact that there's effectively an overfitting
problem, that if you just throw too much context
and the quality of it isn't good, the specificity of it
is not good for the task at hand,
you get poor results out of it.
So getting that right turned out to be a skill that it was worth
building and a platform capability
that was very valuable to us.
And adding that into how we built internally actually
got us to 96% of engineers using AI.
And this would be early 2025.
And we were at a 60% improvement in velocity, so both numbers
up a little bit from where from where they were.
And then when we looked at how we would apply this
to our customers, well, it turns out
across the go-to-market journey, there's
a lot of different things that you need to do
and a lot of different agents, whether it's a prospecting agent
or a customer support agent.
And being able to deliver the right context at the right time
allows you to drive significantly better outcomes
in terms of quality, performance, and cost.
So it was critical there.
And we saw dramatic changes.
For example, an agent that builds an outreach email
as a follow-up to a sales demo went, in about six months,
from a sales rep needing to edit it about 2/3 of the time to make
some changes, to make it in their voice,
or to correct something, to them sending it without any edits 2/3
of the time.
So AI knows a lot about the world,
but you need a platform that knows your world at the end
of the day, your business.
And most of that data is data that
exists only inside of your business and not out
in the world, and therefore in the models.
And the last thing is meet customers where they are.
This was really all about how we actually
took that shared platform.
Internally, that meant taking shared tools,
shared primitives, building on the shared platform.
Every agent anybody builds makes all agents
better because it contributes to the overall context
and the actual agent platform itself.
And what that allowed us to do was
get to, essentially, today, 100% of engineers using
agentic coding to build at HubSpot,
and to give you some other metrics, 73% increase in lines,
lines of code, and a 90% reduction in the time
to first feedback on PRs.
So just that velocity was rising,
even as the quality was rising.
And as I mentioned, reliability actually
went up as well for customers through all of that.
So at the end of the day, we also
then realized that we needed to go and meet customers
where they are with all of this technology.
So as a SaaS vendor, historically, you'd
thought about how do you keep customers inside of our UI?
But we actually let go of that entirely and realized
at the end of the day, the value we needed
to deliver for customers was, how do we
make this intelligence that we build indispensable
wherever they work?
So deeply integrating into Claude and Gemini and ChatGPT,
so the customers get the full power
of our agent platform and our context
right there inside of wherever they might be working.
Of course, many customers still choose
to use the web or mobile UIs, or they use our own Breeze
assistant as well.
But we have full parity across those for customers,
and that turned out to be a huge win for our customers
and for us.
So at the end of the day, it's all about getting the foundation
right.
And what we found is if you don't
get those foundational pieces right,
it does start to plateau out.
But once you start getting them in place,
you get this incredibly powerful compound interest
that starts to deliver incredible value, not only
for how our teams build, but then also
for what we're able to deliver to our customers.
Thanks so much.
